The figure appears to be an example of text content rather than a traditional graphical representation like charts or diagrams. It contains structured information presented as part of what seems to be instructions for evaluating code using large language models (LLMs). The components include sections labeled "Task," which describes the evaluation task, and specific prompts designed to guide LLMs in assessing Python solutions against given problems from MBPP+. There are no visible axes labels or legends since this is textual data.

The main structure shows a detailed prompt template intended for use with CoT (Chain-of-Thought) reasoning processes when evaluating coding tasks. This includes placeholders such as `{problem}` and `{solution}`, indicating where specific problem descriptions and proposed solutions would be inserted during actual evaluations. The layout suggests it's meant to standardize how evaluators approach judging the correctness of generated code outputs by providing clear guidelines on what aspects should be considered—such as whether the solution solves the stated task correctly without introducing new issues or relying excessively on external libraries beyond those allowed in the original problem statement.

This figure consists of multiple bar charts comparing different algorithms across four datasets: SIFT (EM), UQ-V (EM), Audio (EM), and Paper (EM). Each dataset section includes three subplots showing index construction time, peak memory usage during both Index Construction and Query Execution phases, and final index size. The x-axis lists various ANN search methods such as FDANN, CAPS, ACORN, NHQ, UNG, etc., while the y-axes show metrics like seconds for time, gigabytes (GB) for memory or size — with scales varying per subplot to accommodate different magnitudes. For example, in SIFT’s “Index constr. time” chart, some methods exceed 16 seconds whereas others stay under 2; similarly, peak memory usage ranges from near zero over 10 GB depending on method and phase. Overall trends suggest that certain algorithms (e.g., ACORN) often require more resources than others (like NHQ or UNG), especially during query execution in larger datasets like Paper (EM).

This figure consists of four line charts arranged horizontally, each showing Recall@10 versus Queries per Second (QPS) for different selectivity values: 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, and 0.8. The x-axis is labeled “Queries per Second (QPS)” on a logarithmic scale from 10² to 10⁴; the y-axis is labeled “Recall@10” ranging from 0.0 to 1.0. Each chart includes multiple colored lines with markers representing different algorithms: ACORN (lower/upper bound), CAPS, FDANN (filtered/stitched), NHQ (kgraph/nsw), and UNG — as shown in the legend on each subplot. Across all subplots, most methods maintain high recall (~1.0) at low QPS but degrade sharply beyond ~10³–10⁴ QPS, with performance varying by selectivity level. The EM label appears only in the top-right corner of the rightmost chart (Selectivity = 0.8).

This figure consists of two side-by-side bar charts showing the distribution of rewriting numbers for Llama3-8B and GPT-4 models on a task involving adaptive query rewriting selection. The x-axis represents the number of rewrites (1, 2, 3, or 4), while the y-axis shows percentage values ranging from 0% to 55%. For both models, most queries are rewritten either twice or thrice — with Llama3-8B peaking at 49.7% for two rewrites and GPT-4 peaking higher at 51.5% also for three rewrites. The average rewrite number is labeled below each chart: 2.482 for Llama3-8B and 2.455 for GPT-4, indicating that fewer than four rewrites are typically selected after dynamic filtering.

This figure consists of two pie charts showing the distribution of evaluatees when Gemma-2 models act as evaluators. The top chart displays data for "gemma-2-9b-it" with a total of 2873 instances, while the bottom chart shows results for another model version totaling 3329 instances. Both visualizations list various large language models around their perimeters, such as Llama and Claude variants, along with corresponding percentage values representing their share of evaluations. The charts use color-coded slices to represent different proportions, highlighting that certain models like llama-3-70b-instruct occupy larger segments compared to others in the distribution.

This figure consists of five line charts arranged horizontally, each showing Recall@k versus Queries per Second (QPS) for different values of k: 20, 40, 60, 80, and 100. The x-axis is labeled “Queries per Second (OPS)” on a logarithmic scale from 10² to 10⁴; the y-axis ranges from 0.0 to 1.0 and represents recall at varying k values as indicated in each subplot title (“Recall@20”, etc.). Each chart includes multiple colored lines representing different algorithms or methods — such as ACORN (lower/upper bound), CAPS, FDANN (filtered/stitched), NHQ (kgraph/nsw), UNG — with corresponding symbols and colors shown in the legend within each plot. The general trend across all subplots shows that higher QPS correlates with lower recall for most methods, though some algorithms maintain high recall even at elevated query rates. All plots are labeled “EM” in the top-right corner of the rightmost chart, indicating they use EM filtering as noted in the caption.

This figure consists of seven separate line charts arranged horizontally, each representing a different dataset category from SlimPajama (Crawl, Exchange, C4, Github, Wikipedia, ArXiv, Book). Each chart plots word length on the x-axis against coverage percentage on the y-axis. The title above each subplot indicates the total percentage covered by the top 10 most frequent word lengths for that dataset; these values range from 972% to 983%. All seven charts show a steep decline in cumulative coverage as word length increases beyond short words (lengths ≤5), indicating high concentration of vocabulary mass among very short tokens. The curves are monotonically decreasing and convex, reflecting diminishing returns when including longer words for achieving full lexical coverage within each dataset subset.

This figure displays three line charts comparing model performance across different embedding matrix ranks (x-axis) against an unspecified metric on the y-axis ranging from 30 to 70. The legend identifies three methods: Baseline (light blue), Decomposition-only (dark blue with diamond markers), and MEL (green). All lines show increasing values as rank increases, but they start at different points—Baseline starts lowest around 31, while Decomposition-only begins near 44 and MEL near 65. At higher ranks (>800), the Baseline curve rises sharply to nearly 70, whereas Decomposition-only plateaus early above 69 and MEL stays flat after rank ~250. The chart suggests that combining decomposition with Matryoshka Embedding Learning (MEL) yields strong performance even at low ranks compared to baseline or decomposition alone.

This figure is a pie chart showing how different models were evaluated when Gemma-2-2B acted as the evaluator — totaling 1,738 instances across all evaluatees. The largest slice (7.4%) corresponds to “gemma-2b-it” itself, followed by other variants like “claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620” and “gemini-pro”, each with labeled percentages such as 6.9%, 5.2%, etc., along with sample counts in parentheses (e.g., [72], [18]). Smaller slices represent less frequently evaluated models, including many fine-tuned or experimental versions like “llama-3-8b-instruct” and “qwen-vl-chat”, some appearing only once or twice. The chart visually emphasizes that Gemma-2-2B most often evaluates its own variant, but also shows broad coverage across dozens of other models — suggesting diverse evaluation behavior even within a single evaluator setup. All labels are arranged radially around the pie, with model names and their corresponding proportions clearly marked for readability.

This figure contains two types of charts: line plots at the top and bar graphs below them. The upper section shows five Recall@k vs Queries per Second (QPS) curves for k values from 20 to 100 under EMIS filtering, with methods like ACORN, FDANN, NHQ, and UNG compared using different symbols and colors — including lower/upper bounds and stitched variants. The bottom section displays four sets of bar charts corresponding to selectivity levels (0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8), each showing index construction time, peak memory usage during both index build and query execution, and final index size across the same set of algorithms. In all subplots, UNG consistently uses less memory but often has slower construction or higher latency; ACORN tends to be faster in queries while using more memory than some alternatives like NHQ (raw). The overall structure suggests a trade-off analysis between speed, memory footprint, and recall accuracy under varying filter selectivities on the arxiv-for-fanns-medium dataset.

This figure consists of three scatter plots arranged horizontally, labeled "MuSiQue," "FinanceBench," and "BrowseComp-Plus." The vertical axis represents Accuracy (ranging from 0.0 to above 0.5), while the horizontal axes represent Cost per query in USD on a logarithmic scale. A legend at the bottom identifies various data points by shape and color, including methods such as No Retrieval, Per-chunk Summary, Agent Loop, Concatenate, and several METIS configurations using different models like GPT-4 or Llama 3. Each plot features a dashed line labeled "Pareto frontier" that outlines the upper boundary of performance relative to cost for the static design-space sweep. The colored stars representing specific methods are plotted against this background to show their operating points within each workload's efficiency landscape.

This figure displays two side-by-side text blocks labeled "Code Fix PPL with Review Comment" and "Code Fix PPL without Review Comment," illustrating a comparison of input prompts for calculating perplexity (PPL). Both panels contain identical code snippets written in Go, specifically showing logic involving `opts.BeforeWrite` checks. The primary difference lies in the instruction section: the left panel includes a specific review comment asking to disallow reading 'ObjectHandle', while the right panel leaves that field empty. A blue dashed line separates these input sections from the bottom area labeled "Calculate Perplexity."

This figure consists of three scatter plots arranged side-by-side for different datasets: MATH500, MMLU, and MBPP+. Each plot displays "Task Accuracy (%)" on the x-axis and "Self-Preference Ratio (%)" on the y-axis to show a positive correlation between model performance and self-preference. The data points are color-coded by model family (Llama in blue, Gemma in green, Qwen in red) and sized according to parameter count ranging from Small (3B) to Large (70-72B). Dashed trend lines indicate strong correlations with specific coefficients visible for each dataset: $r = 0.801$ for MATH500, $r = 0.817$ for MMLU, and $r = 0.771$ for MBPP+.

This figure consists of three horizontal bar charts arranged side-by-side, each showing "Target@3 uplift (pp)" on its x-axis ranging from 0 to approximately 75+. The y-axes list various intervention types grouped by color-coded categories: Atomic (blue), Block (green), Cross-block (orange), and Realistic (red). Each chart corresponds to a different model — Devstral Small, Gemma 4 31B IT, Qwen3.6 27B/24B Instruct — though the exact mapping isn’t labeled in the image itself. Across all three charts, red bars (“Realistic” interventions) generally show higher uplift values than other categories, especially for items like “Caveat-buried FAQ,” “Popularity-heavy profile,” and “Full-stack realistic.” Blue atomic interventions tend to have lower or more variable uplifts compared to the others.

This figure consists of five separate histograms arranged horizontally side-by-side. Each histogram displays green bars representing frequency on the y-axis against "Pairwise Distances between Sampled Vectors" on the x-axis. The plots are labeled with method names at the top: SIFT, Audio, UQ-V, Paper, and transformer-based (ours). While most datasets show a distribution centered around lower distance values, the "transformer-based (ours)" plot exhibits a distinct peak shifted significantly to the right compared to the others.

This figure consists of four bar charts arranged in a 2x2 grid layout. The top row displays results for "0-shot" and "2-shot" settings across tasks like mean, arc_challenge, arc_easy, and webqs; the bottom row shows similar comparisons but includes additional datasets such as hellaswag, multirc, openbookqa, piqa, race, triviaqa, and winogrande. Each chart plots accuracy (acc) on the y-axis against task names on the x-axis. The legend indicates two main methods — T-Free and Unigram — each with multiple variants labeled by data size: baseline, 5k, 10k, 15k, and 20k, represented by different colors and patterns (solid fill vs. crosshatch). Across all charts, the bars generally show that performance varies slightly across methods and dataset sizes, with no single method consistently dominating — some tasks favor T-Free baselines while others are competitive or better under Unigram variants.

This figure displays three grouped bar charts comparing cost savings across different benchmarks: MuSiQue (left), BrowseComp+ (middle), and FinanceBench (right). The vertical axis represents "Cost saving (%)," while the horizontal axis categorizes data by accuracy goals ("100% Acc Goal," "95% Acc Goal," etc.). A legend at the top identifies four query featurizers: GPT-5-mini, GPT-5-nano, Qwen3.5-9B, and text-embedding-3. The bars include error bars indicating standard deviation, with some hatched sections labeled "n/a" to indicate unreachable goals where no router operating point achieved the required accuracy floor.

This figure illustrates the process of developing Desiview4FT and Desiview4FA models through fine-tuning and alignment techniques using large language models (LLMs). It shows a workflow starting with commit reviews where LLMs generate scores for code fixes both without review comments ("Code Fix PPLs without Review Comments") and with them ("Code Fix PPLs with Review Comments"). The difference in these scores is calculated to determine the "Desiredness Scores" of each comment. These desiredness scores are then used to categorize dataset entries into either Desired or Undesired datasets based on whether their score exceeds zero (DS > 0) or not (DS ≤ 0). Finally, this categorized data feeds back into refining base LLMs via fine-tuning for Desiview4FT and alignment processes leading towards creating the final model known as Desiview4FA.

This figure is a stacked bar chart showing how memory usage breaks down across different components when fine-tuning LLaMA models of varying sizes (7B to 65B parameters). The x-axis lists model sizes with their total parameter counts and approximate GPU VRAM requirements in parentheses, while the y-axis shows percentage breakdowns from 0% to 100%. Each bar is divided into colored segments representing: Model weights (blue), Adapters (red), Weight gradients (yellow), Optimizer state (green), and Input gradient (orange) — as defined by the legend at the top. Numbers inside each segment indicate memory footprint in MB for that component; for example, the 65B model’s blue “Model” section alone uses 37074 MB. The chart visually demonstrates that larger models require significantly more total memory, with optimizer and adapter states growing substantially as model size increases — especially evident between the 13B and 33B bars where green (optimizer) jumps from 1800 to 3510 MB despite similar overall bar heights due to scaling effects.

This figure consists of multiple panels (a–h) that compare untrained neural networks with those pretrained on random noise across two model types: a 2D toy network and a high-dimensional CNN-like architecture. Panels (a) and (e) show schematic diagrams — the former depicts a simple feedforward net receiving “Random noise” inputs and producing binary outputs, while the latter illustrates a deeper convolutional-style network processing 32x32x3 images for 10-class classification. Panels (b), (f) display scatter plots or dot clouds visualizing confidence/softmax probabilities over input space; axes are labeled “Feature 1”, “Feature 2” in (b) and “Readout index” in (f). Boxplots in panels (c, d, g, h) quantify metrics like “Confidence bias” and “Class bias” using box-and-whisker plots with asterisks indicating statistical significance (*), comparing “Untrained” vs. “Randomly pretrained”. The main trend shown is that random noise pretraining reduces confidence variance and class imbalance compared to untrained models — evident in tighter distributions around chance level (dashed line) after pretraining, especially visible in panels c, d, g, h where blue boxes (“Random”) are lower and narrower than gray ones (“Untrained”).

This figure contains four panels (a-d) illustrating concepts and results related to out-of-distribution detection using network confidence. Panel **a** shows a conceptual diagram with example images of cars and cats labeled as "ID Class 0" and "1," alongside scattered points representing OOD data. Panels **b**, **c**, and **d** present quantitative analyses, including histograms comparing density distributions for different pretraining methods (labeled w/o vs w/), ROC curves plotting True positive rate against False positive rate, and boxplots displaying AUROC performance metrics with statistical significance markers (*). The text within the figure identifies specific datasets like CIFAR10 and SVHN used in the experiments.

This figure consists of three scatter plots arranged horizontally under the title "Subjective Tasks from LMArena." The x-axis for all three charts represents Task Accuracy (%), while the y-axes represent Judge Accuracy (%), Self-Preference Ratio (%), and Legitimate Self-Preference Ratio (%) respectively. Each plot displays data points colored by model family (Llama, Gemma, Qwen) with point sizes indicating parameter scale from Small to Large. The visual trend shows a positive correlation between task accuracy and the respective y-axis metrics in all three charts, indicated by upward-sloping dashed lines and reported Pearson r values ranging from 0.649 to 0.959.

This figure illustrates an experimental workflow for evaluating code review methods using large language models (LLMs). It shows two main evaluation paths: one involving manual annotation and data distillation to assess desirability judgment; another focusing on fine-tuning or aligning datasets with specialized LLMs like DesiView4FT/FA. The diagram includes components such as sampled dataset, annotated dataset, various data distillation methods, result visualization via magnifying glass icon, automated evaluation gear symbol, and human evaluation person silhouette. Arrows indicate the flow from raw data through processing steps to final results or evaluations. A question mark labeled “Research Questions” points toward both branches of experimentation — suggesting that this framework addresses multiple research questions related to improving code review quality using distilled datasets and LLMs.

This figure is a confusion matrix comparing LLM sufficiency judgments with human majority votes on evidence quality. The vertical axis (y-axis) represents “LLM” labels: Not Suff and Sufficient; the horizontal axis (x-axis) represents “Human Majority” labels: Not Suff and Sufficient. Four cells show counts: 28 where both agree as Not Suff, 91 where LLM says Not Suff but humans say Sufficient, 9 where LLM says Sufficient but humans say Not Suff, and 92 where both agree as Sufficient. The darkest blue cell (bottom-right) indicates strong agreement when evidence is deemed sufficient by both parties. Lighter shades represent less frequent or disagreeing cases.

The figure shown is an example of text content rather than a visual chart or diagram; specifically, it appears to be a screenshot or textual representation of instructions for evaluating answers from two assistants (Assistant A and Assistant B). The components include placeholders like `{question 1}`, `{answer 1}`, and `{answer 2}` which suggest where specific questions and responses would go. There are no axis labels, legends, method names, numerical data points visible in this image since it's purely textual instruction-based content without any graphical elements such as charts or diagrams. The main structure shows a clear directive for acting impartially when judging the quality of provided answers by selecting one among three options: "A", "T" (tie), or "B".

This figure consists of four hand-drawn diagrams comparing two methods: classic tokenization (left) and T-FREE (right), for both encoding (top row) and decoding (bottom row). The top-left diagram shows how a word like “Hello, world!” is broken into tokens via tokenization, then mapped to embeddings through an embedding lookup table. The top-right diagram illustrates T-FREE’s approach: it breaks text into character trigrams or hashes them, aggregates multiple hashed representations using summation (Σ from i=1 to n), and maps those aggregated vectors to sparse multi-label embeddings — reducing the size of the final representation compared to single-token mappings. In the bottom-left bar chart (“Decode”), probabilities are shown for words in a “single-class vocabulary” where each word corresponds to one entry; bars represent likelihoods across possible outputs like “Sun,” “House,” etc. The bottom-right bar chart shows decoding under T-FREE’s “multi-class vocabulary”: here, overlapping labels (e.g., “mouse House”, “ouse”) indicate that multiple subword units can activate simultaneously during generation — reflecting morphological similarity and enabling compression by sharing activation patterns across related forms.

This figure is an architecture diagram illustrating how Large Language Models (LLMs) generate simulated opinions based on specific roles. The process begins with a top-level "Input Prompt" asking for support of expanding Medicare to cover all Americans. This prompt branches into two distinct paths labeled "Created Roles," which define the personality traits used by the model: one is blue and represents a conservative-leaning persona low in agreeableness, while the other is purple and represents a liberal-leaning persona high in agreeableness. Both role descriptions feed into a central green box containing an LLM icon with gears, indicating that these parameters guide the AI's processing. Finally, arrows point downward to a "Simulated Opinion" block at the bottom, showing where the generated output appears after passing through the model.

This figure consists of seven panels (a–g) that combine biological illustrations and machine learning performance charts to compare neural network training methods. Panel a shows an illustration of spontaneous neural activity before eye opening versus sensory input after eye opening in rats; panel b displays timelines for visual and auditory development relative to birth, with markers like P0, P12, E14, etc.; panels c–g focus on pretraining algorithms: panel c illustrates random noise stimulus feeding into a network architecture producing uniform label distributions (shown as histograms); panels d shows test loss curves over epochs comparing “w/” vs. “w/o” random pretaining; panels e and f present confidence calibration metrics via histogram ratios, reliability diagrams with accuracy vs. confidence plots, and ECE values marked by asterisks indicating statistical significance; panel g uses heatmaps to show how size of training data affects ECE across network depths for both conditions (“w/” blue tones, “w/o” red/orange tones). The main trend is that pretraining with random noise improves calibration — lower test loss (d), tighter confidence-accuracy alignment (e,f), and reduced miscalibration error (g) compared to no pretaining.
